q-74918.name: Question 1
q-74918.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,1,2)}\frac{x{z}^{2}-y{z}^{2}}{yz-xz}=\frac{1\cdot {2}^{2}-1\cdot {2}^{2}}{1\cdot 2-1\cdot 2}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,1,2)}\frac{x{z}^{2}-y{z}^{2}}{yz-xz} & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1,2)}\frac{(x-y){z}^{2}}{(y-x)z} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1,2)}-\frac{(x-y){z}^{2}}{(x-y)z} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1,2)}(-z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,1,2)}(-z) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form 00, as follows:

limx→(1,1,2)xz2−yz2yz−xz=1⋅22−1⋅221⋅2−1⋅2=00

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

limx→(1,1,2)xz2−yz2yz−xz=limx→(1,1,2)(x−y)z2(y−x)z=limx→(1,1,2)−(x−y)z2(x−y)z=limx→(1,1,2)(−z)

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

limx→(1,1,2)(−z)=−2

Therefore, the limit evaluates to −2.

q-74956.name: Question 2
q-74956.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}-1}=\frac{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}-1)(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})^{2}-{1}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1)}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}+1) & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1}+1 \\  & =\sqrt{1}+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $2.$

q-129340.name: Question 3
q-129340.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{3}-xy}{{x}^{3}y} & =\frac{{0}^{3}-2(0)}{{2}^{3}(0)} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{3}-xy}{{x}^{3}y} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{y({y}^{2}-x)}{{x}^{3}y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{\cancel{y}({y}^{2}-x)}{{x}^{3}\cancel{y}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{{x}^{3}} & =\frac{{0}^{2}-2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-\frac{1}{4}.$

q-129342.name: Question 4
q-129342.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}+x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}} & =\frac{\sqrt{0}-\sqrt{0}+0-0}{\sqrt{0}-\sqrt{0}} \\  & =\frac{0-0+0-0}{0-0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}+x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}} & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}+x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})+(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{x-y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{x-y+(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{x-y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{(x-y)(1+\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{x-y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\cancel{(x-y)}(1+\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{\cancel{x-y}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}(1+\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}(1+\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}) & =1+\sqrt{0}+\sqrt{0} \\  & =1+0+0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $1.$

Question 4
?

limx→(0,0)x−y+x−yx−y=

a
0
b
2
c
1
d
12
e
14
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form 00, as follows: limx→(0,0)x−y+x−yx−y=0−0+0−00−0=0−0+0−00−0=00

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator: limx→(0,0)x−y+x−yx−y=limx→(0,0)(x−y+x−y)(x+y)(x−y)(x+y)=limx→(0,0)(x−y)(x+y)+(x−y)(x+y)x−y=limx→(0,0)x−y+(x−y)(x+y)x−y=limx→(0,0)(x−y)(1+x+y)x−y=limx→(0,0)(x−y)(1+x+y)x−y=limx→(0,0)(1+x+y)

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it: limx→(0,0)(1+x+y)=1+0+0=1+0+0=1

Therefore, the limit evaluates to 1.

q-129401.name: Question 5
q-129401.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & =\frac{{0}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(1,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (1,0)$ along the path $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)\,\,\,y=0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{0}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (1,0)$ along the path $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)\,\,\,x=1}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}=\text{DNE}
$$

EXPLANATION

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form 00: limx→(1,0)y2x2+y2−1=0212+02−1=01−1=00

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching (1,0) from different paths.

  • Taking x→(1,0) along the path y=0, we have limx→(1,0)y=0y2x2+y2−1=limx→102x2+02−1=limx→10=0.

  • Taking x→(1,0) along the path x=1, we have limx→(1,0)x=1y2x2+y2−1=limy→0y212+y2−1=limy→0y2y2=limy→01=1
